title: Subarray Product Less Than K
description:
# Subarray Product Less Than K

Given an array of positive integers `nums` and an integer `k`, return the number of non-empty contiguous subarrays where the product of all elements in the subarray is strictly less than `k`.

The inequality is strict: a product equal to `k` does not count.

## Example 1:

**Input:** nums = [10,5,2,6], k = 100
**Output:** 8
**Explanation:** The valid subarrays are `[10]`, `[5]`, `[2]`, `[6]`, `[10,5]`, `[5,2]`, `[2,6]`, and `[5,2,6]`.

## Example 2:

**Input:** nums = [1,2,3], k = 0
**Output:** 0
**Explanation:** Every product is positive, so no subarray can have product less than `0`.

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= nums.length <= 3 * 10^4`
*   `1 <= nums[i] <= 1000`
*   `0 <= k <= 10^6`

solutions.name: Sliding Window Product
solutions.description:
## Approach
Use a two-pointer window whose product is always less than `k` after shrinking. Extend the right end by multiplying `nums[right]`. While the product is too large, divide out `nums[left]` and move `left` forward. Once valid, every subarray ending at `right` and starting from `left` through `right` is valid.

## Key Insight
All numbers are positive, so extending the window never decreases the product and removing elements from the left never increases it. That monotonic behavior is exactly what makes a sliding window correct.

## Complexity Analysis
Each index enters and leaves the window at most once, so the time complexity is `O(n)`. The algorithm uses `O(1)` extra space.

solutions.name: Reset-Aware Sliding Window
solutions.description:
## Approach
This is the same window invariant, but it treats any single value `>= k` as a hard separator. Such a value cannot belong to any valid subarray, so the product is reset and the next window starts after it. Inside each clean segment, the usual product window counts valid endings.

## Key Insight
When `k > 1`, every valid subarray must avoid values that are already at least `k`. Making that reset explicit helps prevent off-by-one mistakes around single invalid elements and product equality.

## Complexity Analysis
Every element is processed a constant number of times, so the time complexity is `O(n)`. Only a few counters are stored, so the space complexity is `O(1)`.

solutions.name: Prefix Log Binary Search
solutions.description:
## Approach
Convert products to sums of logarithms. A subarray product `nums[start..end]` is less than `k` exactly when `logPrefix[end + 1] - logPrefix[start] < log(k)`. For each start index, binary search the largest prefix index that still satisfies this inequality.

## Key Insight
Logs turn multiplication into addition, and all values are positive, so the prefix-log array is nondecreasing. This gives an alternate binary-search route and also reinforces why strict `< k` needs a small epsilon around equality.

## Complexity Analysis
Building the prefix-log array costs `O(n)`. Running one binary search per start costs `O(n log n)` total time, and the prefix array uses `O(n)` space.

solutions.name: Brute Force With Early Break
solutions.description:
## Approach
Enumerate every start index, multiply values while extending the end index, and stop as soon as the product reaches or exceeds `k`. Every product observed before that break is a valid subarray.

## Key Insight
Because every value is positive, once a growing product is no longer less than `k`, extending it farther cannot make it valid again. That gives a simple correctness baseline and explains the monotonicity used by the sliding window.

## Complexity Analysis
In the worst case, many products stay below `k`, so the nested loops take `O(n^2)` time. Only the running product and answer are stored, so the space complexity is `O(1)`.
